items.title: 17.2 Relation Between Mean Power and Maximum Power for an Alternating Current

source_refs.note: Topic 17.2 with Example 17.2 and boxes (PDF 89-90); Fig 17.4 redrawn; clamp meter and blood-sugar photographs described. A note gives the rms reading of Example 17.2. The check question is added.

blocks.text: An alternating current periodically reverses direction, so the voltage and current vary sinusoidally. A resistive load is one that does not store energy (as a capacitor or inductor does) but simply dissipates it as heat. The instantaneous power in a circuit is the power at any moment: P = VI (17.5). The maximum (peak) power occurs when the current and voltage are at their peak values Io and Vo; the mean power is the average over one complete cycle (Fig 17.4).

For a sinusoidal AC in a resistor R, the maximum power is Pmax = Io^2 R (17.6) and the mean power is Pmean = Irms^2 R (17.7). Since Io = square root of 2 x Irms, Pmax = 2 Irms^2 R = 2 Pmean, so Pmean = Pmax / 2 (17.8). The mean power in a resistive load is half the maximum power: the instantaneous power reaches its maximum at certain points of the cycle but spends a lot of time at lower values, down to zero.

blocks.alt: A graph of power against time: a red curve rises from zero to the maximum line, falls back to zero and repeats, staying above zero; it peaks twice for each cycle of the dashed blue current shown for reference. Dashed lines mark the maximum power Pmax = VoIo = Io^2 R and the mean power Pmean = (1/2)Pmax = Irms^2 R, halfway up.
blocks.caption: Power in a resistor carrying AC (original graph after Fig 17.4).
blocks.long_description: Because power depends on the square of the current, it is positive in both half-cycles. Its average is exactly half its peak, which is why rms values are peak values divided by the square root of 2.

blocks.text: An alternating voltage of 220 V is applied across a 50 ohm resistor. Find the mean power in kilowatts, treating 220 V as the peak value as the book does. Solution: Pmax = V^2 / R = (220 V)^2 / 50 ohm = 968 W. The mean power is half: Pmean = 968 W / 2 = 484 W = 0.484 kW.

blocks.title: Peak or rms?
blocks.text: Mains voltages are normally quoted as rms values. If the 220 V in Example 17.2 were the rms value, the mean power would be Vrms^2 / R = (220 V)^2 / 50 ohm = 968 W, and the peak power 1936 W.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: A digital clamp meter measures AC and DC currents without breaking the circuit: its jaws close around a single wire and sense the magnetic field of the current. (The book also shows a photograph captioned 'scientists have converted human blood sugar into electricity'.)

blocks.prompt: A resistor dissipates a peak power of 200 W in an AC circuit. What is its mean power?

items: P = VI at each instant; Pmax = Io^2 R; Pmean = Irms^2 R.
